sections.overview: Native to East Asia, especially China, this freshwater carp was selectively bred into an ornamental fish now kept worldwide. Selective breeding in China for more than a thousand years produced colours and body forms that were later spread through the ornamental trade.
sections.identification: The wild-looking form is elongated, bronze-grey and single-tailed; ordinary domestic fish retain this shape but are often orange. Adults commonly reach 20 cm, though exceptional wild or pond fish approach 45 cm. Lifespan varies; reports beyond 40 years are exceptional, not normal. Selected varieties may have a rounded body, double tail, enlarged eyes or head growths, and some lack a dorsal fin; these traits differ from the ordinary single-tailed form. Wild and feral fish typically reach 12–22 cm standard length and 100–300 g; exceptional records reach 41 cm standard length and about 3 kg. Standard length excludes the tail fin.
sections.habitat: It inhabits temperate ponds, lakes, wetlands and slow rivers; introductions have spread it beyond East Asia. It can survive temporary oxygen deprivation, especially in cold conditions, using stored energy; survival becomes shorter at higher temperatures.
sections.diet: Omnivorous, it eats algae, plants, insect larvae, crustaceans, eggs and detritus. It sucks up food and sediment, sorting particles before pharyngeal processing. A muscular structure in the roof of its mouth, the palatal organ, detects particles through taste and helps separate edible material from gravel before swallowing. The rejected gravel is spat out, so movements that resemble chewing can instead be the sorting of a mixed mouthful of food and substrate.
sections.behavior: It schools loosely, learns feeding cues and remembers learned associations, disproving the three-second memory myth.
sections.reproduction: At spring spawning, males chase females; eggs stick to plants and sperm fertilizes them externally. Fry hatch in about two to nine days, without parental care. Hatchlings are about 5 mm, dark at first, and mature after three to four years.
sections.ecology: Goldfish eat aquatic animals and native fish eggs; introduced populations compete with local fish and disturb bottom habitats while feeding. Bottom feeding can uproot plants and resuspend sediments, increasing water turbidity and changing conditions for other aquatic organisms.
sections.conservation: IUCN’s global 2013 assessment classed it Least Concern. Released fish are invasive in some regions.
